title: Barriers 2024 — Part B
source: WSU Y5 Barriers 2024 MCQ, student reconstruction; stems rewritten, tested point preserved

questions.stem: A 23-year-old student has a week of pain in the left wrist, both knees and an ankle, intermittent fevers and some dysuria. Multiple sexual partners, no trauma.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Asymmetric oligoarthritis after urethritis in a young sexually active adult is reactive arthritis (chlamydia). Gonococcal arthritis is the alternative — migratory, with tenosynovitis and pustular rash — and both need STI testing.
questions.point: Asymmetric lower-limb oligoarthritis with recent urethritis or diarrhoea in a young adult is reactive arthritis; test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea either way.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with fatigue: TSH 14 mU/L (0.3–3.5), free T4 8 pmol/L (10–25), free T3 5 pmol/L (3.5–7.5).
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: High TSH with low T4 is primary hypothyroidism, and Hashimoto's is its commonest cause. Secondary would have a low/normal TSH; sick euthyroid drops T3 first with a normal-ish TSH.
questions.point: Raised TSH with low free T4 = primary hypothyroidism, most commonly Hashimoto's; a low or inappropriately normal TSH with low T4 points to the pituitary.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has weight loss, thirst and nocturia. Na 151 (135–145), serum osmolality 312 (280–300), fasting glucose 5.8, urine osmolality 150 mmol/kg.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypernatraemia and high serum osmolality with inappropriately dilute urine is DI — the kidney fails to concentrate. Normal glucose excludes DM; primary polydipsia gives a low sodium.
questions.point: High serum osmolality and sodium with dilute urine (<300 mmol/kg) = diabetes insipidus; primary polydipsia has low-normal sodium, and SIADH the reverse pattern.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has 6 months of worsening balance with falls, mostly at night in the bathroom. He stands with feet together eyes open but falls when they close. Vestibulo-ocular reflexes are intact.
questions.lead: Where is the pathology?
questions.explanation: Steady with eyes open, unsteady with eyes closed = positive Romberg = sensory ataxia (proprioception). Cerebellar ataxia is unsteady eyes open too; intact VOR excludes vestibular. Falls in the dark clinch it — peripheral neuropathy or dorsal columns.
questions.point: Positive Romberg (steady eyes open, falls eyes closed) is proprioceptive loss — peripheral neuropathy or dorsal columns; cerebellar ataxia is unsteady with eyes open too.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old nursing home resident with osteoporosis is vitamin D deficient with a normal serum calcium.
questions.lead: What compensatory mechanism keeps the calcium normal?
questions.explanation: Vitamin D deficiency lowers gut calcium absorption; secondary hyperparathyroidism mobilises bone to hold serum calcium — at the cost of the skeleton. The normal calcium is the sign of compensation, not health.
questions.point: In vitamin D deficiency a normal calcium is maintained by secondary hyperparathyroidism (raised PTH mobilising bone) — the normal value is itself the abnormal finding.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with pleuritic chest pain: no PMH, no immobilisation, HR 70, SpO2 94%, normal CXR, ABG and ECG.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate initial test?
questions.explanation: Low pre-test probability (Wells low, PERC not fully negative because of age/sats) → D-dimer to exclude PE. CTPA is for high probability or a positive D-dimer.
questions.point: Suspected PE with low pre-test probability: D-dimer first (a negative result excludes it); go straight to CTPA only when probability is high.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes is having a bowel resection today. No insulin taken; admission glucose 5.5.
questions.lead: How is her diabetes best managed perioperatively?
options: Normal saline with IV insulin infusion
Half her usual basal dose subcutaneously
questions.explanation: Type 1 patients always need insulin — withholding it risks DKA within hours. Fasting means giving substrate too: dextrose with a variable-rate insulin infusion, glucose checked hourly.
questions.point: Type 1 diabetes perioperatively: never withhold insulin — run a variable-rate insulin infusion with dextrose while fasting to prevent DKA and hypoglycaemia.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old man has 6 weeks of constant low back pain unresponsive to paracetamol and NSAID, present at rest and disturbing sleep. ESR 70, urea 9.6, creatinine 125, total protein 86 (64–83), albumin 36, corrected calcium 2.65 (2.15–2.55), PSA 2.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rest pain, high ESR, raised total protein with normal albumin (a paraprotein gap), hypercalcaemia and renal impairment — myeloma. Order serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains.
questions.point: Back pain at rest with high ESR, a protein–albumin gap, hypercalcaemia and renal impairment is myeloma — send SPEP and serum free light chains.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has 3 days of an acutely painful, swollen right wrist without trauma. Last year she had a swollen first MTP that settled over weeks. No other joints involved.
questions.lead: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A prior self-limiting podagra episode plus a new monoarthritis is gout. RA is symmetrical, small-joint and persistent. Aspirate if in doubt — septic arthritis is the one you cannot afford to miss.
questions.point: Recurrent acute monoarthritis with a previous first-MTP episode is gout; aspirate a hot joint to confirm crystals and exclude sepsis.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with a positive pregnancy test at 7 weeks has followed a strict vegan diet for 6 years.
questions.lead: Which nutrient is most important to check?
questions.explanation: Long-term veganism reliably depletes B12 (animal-source only); deficiency causes maternal anaemia and fetal neural tube and neurodevelopmental harm.
questions.point: A long-term vegan in early pregnancy needs B12 checked and supplemented — it is the nutrient absent from plant foods and matters for the fetal nervous system.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old was punched in the face last night. He has infraorbital bruising, numbness of the cheek below the eye, and diplopia on upward gaze.
questions.lead: What is the cause of the diplopia?
options: Inferior rectus entrapment in an orbital floor fracture
questions.explanation: Blowout fracture: the floor gives way, trapping inferior rectus (can't look up) and injuring the infraorbital nerve (cheek numbness). CT orbits, ophthalmology and maxillofacial referral.
questions.point: Orbital floor blowout fracture = diplopia on upward gaze (inferior rectus entrapment) plus infraorbital nerve numbness of the cheek.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman is 10 weeks pregnant.
questions.lead: Which vaccine combination is appropriate during this pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Inactivated vaccines are safe: influenza any trimester, dTpa 20–32 weeks for pertussis antibody transfer. MMR and varicella are live and contraindicated in pregnancy.
questions.point: In pregnancy give influenza (any trimester) and dTpa (20–32 weeks); live vaccines — MMR, varicella — are contraindicated.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old woman has 2 weeks of jaw pain on chewing that eases when she stops, 10 days of new headache, and two days of transient dimming of vision in the left eye.
questions.lead: Which medication should be started?
questions.explanation: Jaw claudication + new headache + amaurosis in an older patient is giant cell arteritis with impending visual loss. Steroids now, ESR/CRP and temporal artery biopsy after — never wait for the biopsy.
questions.point: Jaw claudication, new headache and transient visual loss over 50 = giant cell arteritis: start high-dose steroids immediately, biopsy afterwards.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man has 2 days of right ear pain and discharge with reduced hearing. Pulling the pinna is very painful; the canal is oedematous with yellow slough and the drum cannot be seen.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Tragal/pinna tenderness with an oedematous canal is otitis externa — topical treatment (aural toilet plus combination drops). Oral antibiotics are for spreading cellulitis or immunocompromise.
questions.point: Painful pinna traction with an oedematous, sloughy canal = otitis externa — treat topically (aural toilet, antibiotic/steroid drops), not with oral antibiotics.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old breastfeeding a 5-week-old has 3 days of left breast pain and fever. There is a tender, non-fluctuant mass with overlying erythema. Frequent feeding and expression have not helped.
questions.lead: What is the next step?
options: Breast ultrasound to look for abscess
questions.explanation: Mastitis that fails conservative measures with a mass needs ultrasound to find the abscess (fluctuance is unreliable early); drainage plus antibiotics follows. Continue feeding.
questions.point: Mastitis with a mass that has not settled with feeding/expression: ultrasound for abscess (fluctuance is unreliable), then aspirate/drain plus flucloxacillin, and keep breastfeeding.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT assessed when determining a patient's capacity to consent?
questions.lead: Choose one.
options: Ability to weigh the risks and benefits
questions.explanation: Capacity is understand, retain, weigh, communicate. Written form is documentation, not capacity — a valid verbal consent from a capable patient is consent.
questions.point: Capacity to consent = understand, retain, weigh, communicate; a signature is documentation, not a component of capacity.

questions.stem: Which best describes metformin's mechanism in type 2 diabetes?
questions.lead: Choose one.
options: Decreases hepatic glucose production and decreases insulin resistance
Increases insulin secretion from beta cells
Increases hepatic glucose production and decreases insulin resistance
questions.explanation: Metformin reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and improves peripheral insulin sensitivity; it does not drive insulin release, so no hypoglycaemia. Sulfonylureas secrete; SGLT2 inhibitors excrete; acarbose delays absorption.
questions.point: Metformin lowers hepatic glucose output and improves insulin sensitivity without stimulating insulin secretion — hence no hypoglycaemia; sulfonylureas secrete, SGLT2 inhibitors excrete.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man has burning back pain after lifting cement, radiating to the anterior knee and medial leg. Knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion are weak, the right knee jerk is absent, and pinprick is reduced over the knee and medial leg.
questions.lead: Which nerve root is compressed?
questions.explanation: Absent knee jerk with medial leg sensory loss is L4 (dorsiflexion weakness overlaps L4/L5). L5 has no reflex and lateral leg/dorsum sensation; S1 is the ankle jerk.
questions.point: L4 radiculopathy = absent knee jerk, weak knee extension/dorsiflexion, medial leg numbness; L5 has no reflex loss and affects the great toe and dorsum.

questions.stem: According to the Australian Diabetes Handbook, what is the general HbA1c target for people with type 2 diabetes?
questions.lead: Choose one.
questions.explanation: The general target is ≤7% (53 mmol/mol), individualised — tighter (≤6.5%) if achievable safely early in disease, looser (≤8%) in the frail or hypoglycaemia-prone.
questions.point: General HbA1c target in T2DM is ≤7% (53 mmol/mol), individualised: tighter early if safe, looser (≤8%) in the frail or those at hypoglycaemia risk.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man is in recovery after a cardiac procedure complicated by right ventricular puncture.
questions.lead: Which finding is distinctive for cardiac tamponade?
questions.explanation: Tamponade: Beck's triad (hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds) with pulsus paradoxus — a >10 mmHg inspiratory fall in systolic BP — and tachycardia. Treatment is pericardiocentesis.
questions.point: Cardiac tamponade = hypotension, raised JVP, muffled sounds (Beck's triad) plus pulsus paradoxus and tachycardia; needs urgent pericardiocentesis.
